Testicular pain

Two sham-controlled trials reported lower pain and higher sexual-satisfaction scores after PBM in chronic testicular pain, including a separate post-varicocelectomy cohort. Both were small and conducted by one research group.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two sham-controlled trials reported lower pain and higher sexual-satisfaction scores after PBM in chronic testicular pain, including a separate post-varicocelectomy cohort. Both were small and conducted by one research group.

Summary of the Evidence

Two randomized, sham-controlled human trials were identified, with 60 participants in each. One enrolled men with chronic testicular pain and excluded varicocele and previous varicocele surgery. The other enrolled a distinct group with pain after varicocelectomy; it is also listed separately in the following indication row, so that cross-listing is not a third cohort. Both trials came from the same Iranian research group. No animal or in-vitro study of testicular pain was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

In the chronic-pain trial, 60 participants were assigned to red laser, near-infrared laser, or sham treatment. Both active groups had lower pain scores and higher sexual-satisfaction scores than sham at six and twelve weeks from treatment start. The study followed participants for a limited period after the 12-session course, so it does not establish long-term recurrence or function (Momenzadeh et al. 2024).

The second trial enrolled 60 men with orchialgia following varicocelectomy. It also reported reduced pain and increased sexual satisfaction in the red- and near-infrared groups relative to sham during its reported follow-up (Momenzadeh et al. 2024). Although the cohorts were distinct, authorship and treatment design were closely related, so independent replication remains important.

Animal evidence

No animal experiment directly testing PBM for testicular pain was identified. Animal studies of testicular injury or hormones were not treated as pain studies.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or tissue study directly assessing testicular pain was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Both trials compared 650-nm red visible light at 50 mW with 820-nm near-infrared light at 100 mW and sham. Treatment was applied bilaterally by probe contact to three points near the upper scrotal nerve, for 15 minutes three times weekly over 12 sessions. The protocols differ in their study populations and follow-up. Because wavelength and output power varied together, the trials do not isolate which parameter accounts for the observed pain changes.

Interpretation

Two small sham-controlled trials reported short-term improvements in pain and sexual-satisfaction scores. The separate postoperative cohort adds direct evidence for pain after varicocelectomy, while the single research group and limited follow-up constrain generalization. Independent replication with longer follow-up and functional outcomes would clarify how durable the reported relief is.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term pain reduction and sexual satisfaction
Publications and records2 distinct randomized cohorts

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Both sham-controlled trials reported lower pain scores and higher sexual satisfaction through their short-term follow-up, but each enrolled only 60 patients and both came from one Iranian research group. Replication by independent centers, with a larger sample and follow-up beyond 12 weeks, would show whether the improvement is reliable and lasts.
